summary:
Samsun is a province on Turkey's Black Sea coast. No province-specific rule, ban or enforcement programme governing transgender visitors is recorded there. What a trans visitor to Samsun faces is the national framework, which applies in the province as in every other.

That framework is contradictory on its face. Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858 and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, yet legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Article 40 of the Civil Code, with the applicant at least 18 years old, unmarried, and holding a medical report issued by a state-designated hospital. A visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation is therefore dealing with a country in which recognised gender change is possible but slow, court-gated and medically conditioned.

The direction of travel is restrictive. A leaked 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 and analysed in an Amnesty International factsheet published the following month, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, and penalise participation in same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, impose mandatory infertility and multi-evaluation hurdles, imprison providers for up to 7 years and patients for up to 3 years, and raise the minimum age for legal gender recognition procedures from 18 to 25 with further conditions added. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association have objected. The draft is 66 pages long, amends the Turkish Penal Code, the Civil Code and six other laws, and was leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025; it is the third set of proposed legal amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights in 2025, the earlier two having stalled in Parliament. The proposals are nationwide and would apply within Samsun as in every other province.

The Turkish military bars homosexuals from service and treats homosexuality as a "psychosexual" illness.
tangentialFactors:
Istanbul Pride drew roughly 100,000 participants in 2013-2014, and the 2015-2018 parades were banned by local authorities. Samsun has no recorded Pride event of comparable scale in the inventory, but the national pattern of Pride bans is relevant context for any public visibility.

Amnesty International's November 2025 factsheet warns that the leaked draft would criminalise LGBTI+ people and those advocating for their rights, and would severely restrict or make impossible trans and gender-diverse people's access to gender-affirming healthcare. The proposals' status as a leaked draft rather than enacted law is itself a factor: two prior packages stalled in Parliament, so the current legal position may differ from the draft text.
localsOnly:
Samsun's residents are subject to the same national provisions as its visitors: Civil Code Article 40's court-gated, unmarried, medical-report requirement for legal gender recognition; the military's exclusion of homosexuals and classification of homosexuality as a "psychosexual" illness; and, if enacted, the 11th Judicial Package's raised ages and criminal penalties for gender-affirming care and legal gender recognition.

No province-specific rule governs Samsun; these provisions apply nationwide to Samsun's residents and visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 11th Judicial Package is a leaked draft, not enacted law as of the reporting dates (mid-October 2025 leak; HRW 29 October 2025; Amnesty November 2025). Whether it has since been passed or further amended is unresolved in the sources provided.

No Samsun-specific enforcement data, detention records, or facility conditions are sourced here; the inventory records only that no province-specific rule exists. Local police practice in Samsun is not documented in these materials.

The inventory does not state whether Samsun has a functioning LGBTI+ civil-society presence or access points for a visitor needing assistance.
